concepts.title: Three ways to put information on a carrier
body: A carrier by itself is a steady sine wave that carries no information. Modulation means changing something about that wave in step with your voice or data. A sine wave has only three things you can change: its strength, its frequency, and its phase.
• Amplitude modulation (AM) varies the strength of the wave, so the instantaneous power level of the RF signal rises and falls with the audio.
• Frequency modulation (FM) varies the instantaneous frequency of the wave, pushing it a little above and below its resting frequency.
• Phase modulation (PM) varies the phase angle of the wave, nudging each cycle a little earlier or later than it would otherwise arrive.

The correct names are simply amplitude, frequency, and phase modulation. Words like convolution, transformation, conversion, or inversion describe other things, not the process of conveying information. Frequency conversion, for example, is what a mixer does, not a way to modulate.

concepts.title: The reactance modulator: FM or PM depending on where it sits
body: A reactance modulator is a circuit (often a varactor diode, whose capacitance changes with voltage) that changes the reactance of a tuned circuit in step with the audio.

Where it is connected decides what you get. Attached to the oscillator, it changes the frequency the oscillator produces, giving true FM. Attached to an RF amplifier stage after the oscillator, it cannot change the oscillator's frequency; it only shifts the timing, or phase, of the signal passing through. That produces phase modulation.
PM and FM sound alike on a receiver, so many VHF FM radios actually generate PM this way. For the exam: reactance modulator on an RF amplifier stage means phase modulation.

concepts.title: The modulation envelope, overmodulation, and flat-topping
body: Look at an AM or SSB signal on an oscilloscope and you see a blur of fast RF cycles whose height rises and falls. Draw a line connecting the tops of all those peaks and you have traced the modulation envelope. It is a picture of the audio riding on the carrier.

Overmodulation means driving the modulation harder than the transmitter can cleanly follow. The envelope gets distorted, and distortion creates new frequencies that the audio never contained. Those extra products spread out on both sides of the signal, so the main effect of overmodulation is excessive bandwidth, often called splatter, which interferes with nearby stations.

Flat-topping is one common form of this. When the microphone gain or drive is set too high, the peaks try to go beyond what the amplifier can deliver and get chopped flat. Flat tops on the envelope mean distortion from excessive drive or speech levels, not a properly adjusted ALC or a well-suppressed carrier.

concepts.title: Which voice mode is narrowest
body: An AM signal has a carrier plus two sidebands, one above and one below. Each sideband is a complete copy of the audio, so AM takes about twice the highest audio frequency, roughly 6 kHz for voice.
Single sideband (SSB) removes the carrier and one of the two sidebands, keeping only one copy of the audio. That makes it the narrowest common phone mode, about 2.4 to 3 kHz wide.

Vestigial sideband keeps one full sideband plus a trimmed-down piece (a vestige) of the other; it was used for analog TV and is wider than SSB. FM and PM voice signals are wider still, typically 10 to 16 kHz.

concepts.title: Frequency shift keying and FT8
body: Frequency shift keying (FSK) sends data by switching the signal between different frequencies. Simple binary FSK uses two frequencies, one for a 1 and one for a 0.

There are two ways to make FSK. Direct FSK changes the transmitter oscillator's frequency directly with the digital control signal, so the RF itself jumps between two frequencies. Audio FSK (AFSK) instead feeds two audio tones into an SSB transmitter, which shifts them up to RF. Either way the result on the air looks alike.

FSK does not have to stop at two tones. FT8, the popular weak-signal mode, uses 8-tone frequency shift keying: each symbol is one of eight closely spaced tones, so each tone carries three bits. The whole signal is only about 50 Hz wide.

concepts.title: Phase shift keying: BPSK and QPSK
body: Phase shift keying (PSK) sends data by changing the phase of the carrier. Binary PSK (BPSK) uses two phases, 180 degrees apart, so each symbol carries one bit.
Quadrature PSK (QPSK) uses four phases: 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees. With four possible states, each symbol carries a pair of bits.

QPSK31 is the four-phase version of the PSK31 keyboard mode. It runs at the same symbol rate as BPSK31, so its bandwidth is about the same. It uses the extra bit in each symbol to add error-correcting code. And it is sideband sensitive: flipping between upper and lower sideband mirrors the signal, turning a 90 degree shift into a 270 degree shift, so both stations must use the same sideband. BPSK31 does not care, because 180 degrees looks the same either way.

concepts.title: Link budgets and link margin
body: A link budget is an accounting of everything that happens to your signal between transmitter and receiver, usually worked in decibels so everything just adds and subtracts. Start with the transmitter power, add the gain of the transmitting and receiving antennas, then subtract the losses: feed line loss at both ends, path loss through space, connectors, and so on. The result is the signal power that actually arrives at the receiver.

Link margin is how much extra you have. It is the difference between that received power level and the minimum signal the receiver needs at its input to work properly. A positive margin gives you a cushion against fading and bad conditions; zero margin means the link barely works.
Watch the tempting shortcuts: transmit power minus receiver sensitivity ignores all the gains and losses in between, and a link budget has nothing to do with money.
concepts.formula: Received power = TX power + antenna gains − losses; Link margin = received power − minimum required signal

concepts.title: Mixers, heterodyning, and the local oscillator
body: A mixer takes two signals and combines them in a non-linear circuit. The output contains the sum and the difference of the two input frequencies (plus the originals and some weaker extras). Mixing two RF signals is also called heterodyning, which is why a superheterodyne receiver has that name.

In a receiver, one mixer input is the incoming RF signal and the other is a local oscillator (LO) inside the radio. The radio picks out one of the mixing products, usually the difference, as a fixed intermediate frequency (IF), where most of the filtering and amplifying is done.

Because the IF is fixed, tuning the receiver means changing the local oscillator. Move the LO and a different incoming frequency now lands on the IF. Example: with a 9 MHz IF, an LO at 23.2 MHz converts 14.2 MHz to 9 MHz (23.2 − 14.2 = 9).
concepts.formula: Mixer output = LO + RF and LO − RF

concepts.title: Image response
body: A mixer cannot tell which side of the local oscillator a signal came from. A signal the IF distance below the LO and one the IF distance above it both produce the same difference frequency. One is the signal you want; the other is called the image.

Since the wanted signal and the image sit on opposite sides of the LO, each one IF away, they are separated by twice the IF. Example: IF 9 MHz, LO 23.2 MHz. The desired 14.2 MHz gives 9 MHz, but so does 32.2 MHz (32.2 − 23.2 = 9). 32.2 − 14.2 = 18 MHz, which is twice the IF.
Interference from that unwanted signal is called image response. Filtering ahead of the mixer, to keep the image frequency out, is the cure.

concepts.title: Frequency multipliers and deviation
body: Many VHF FM transmitters generate their signal at a lower frequency, where stable oscillators are easy to build, and then use a multiplier stage to reach the operating frequency. A multiplier is an amplifier run in a non-linear way so it creates harmonics, followed by a tuned circuit that picks out the wanted one (for example the 3rd or 12th harmonic).
Multiplying the frequency also multiplies the deviation. If the oscillator swings 400 Hz and the signal is multiplied 12 times, the output swings 12 × 400 = 4800 Hz.
So to find how much deviation the oscillator needs, first find the multiplication factor (output frequency ÷ oscillator frequency), then divide the desired final deviation by that factor.
concepts.formula: Oscillator deviation = final deviation ÷ (output frequency ÷ oscillator frequency)

concepts.title: FM bandwidth: Carson's rule
body: Deviation is how far an FM signal swings away from its center frequency. But the signal takes up more room than just the deviation, because the audio creates sidebands spaced at the audio frequency out beyond the deviation.

A handy estimate, called Carson's rule, covers almost all of the signal's energy: add the deviation and the highest modulating (audio) frequency, then double the total to account for both sides of center.
Example: 5 kHz deviation with 3 kHz audio gives 2 × (5 + 3) = 16 kHz. Answers of 5 or 8 kHz forget either the audio or the doubling.

concepts.title: Intermodulation and odd-order products
body: Intermodulation happens when two or more signals pass through a non-linear circuit, such as an overloaded receiver front end or a corroded connection, and mix together to create unwanted spurious signals. It is the same physics as a mixer, but unintended. Heterodyning is the deliberate version.

Each product has the form (m × F1) ± (n × F2). Its order is m + n, found by adding the multipliers and ignoring the signs. So 2F1 − F2 is third order (2 + 1), 3F1 − F2 is fourth order (3 + 1), and 5F1 − 3F2 is eighth order (5 + 3).

Odd-order products of the difference type (like 2F1 − F2 and 2F2 − F1) land right next to the original signals, often inside the same band, which makes them the troublemakers. Even-order products fall far away (near 2F1, F1 + F2, or F2 − F1) and are easy to filter out. Example: 14.100 and 14.110 MHz give third-order products at 14.090 and 14.120 MHz.
concepts.formula: Order of (m × F1 ± n × F2) = m + n

concepts.title: Duty cycle and your transmitter's ratings
body: Duty cycle is the portion of the time the transmitter is putting out full power while you are transmitting. SSB voice has a low duty cycle, because speech has pauses and peaks, so average power is well below peak. CW is keyed on and off, so it runs roughly half the time.

Modes like FM, RTTY, and FT8 are key-down at full power for the whole transmission, a duty cycle near 100 percent. A transmitter or amplifier rated 100 watts for SSB may overheat if run at 100 watts continuously on these modes.
Knowing the duty cycle lets you keep the average power within the transmitter's rating, usually by turning the power down for high-duty-cycle modes.

concepts.title: Receiver bandwidth and symbol rate
body: Noise is spread across every frequency, so the wider your receiver's filter, the more noise it lets in. The best signal-to-noise ratio comes when the receiver bandwidth matches the signal: wide enough to pass all of it, and no wider. That is why you use a narrow filter for CW and a wider one for SSB. No FCC rule requires this; it is just good receiving.

For digital modes, the symbol rate (how many symbols per second are sent) sets the bandwidth. Changing faster means the signal needs more room, so higher symbol rates require wider bandwidth. A slow mode like PSK31 at 31.25 symbols per second is very narrow; a fast data mode is wide.

concepts.title: RTTY, Baudot code, mark and space
body: Radioteletype (RTTY) is the oldest ham keyboard mode. It uses Baudot code (also called ITA2), in which each character is 5 bits. Five bits only give 32 combinations, so special shift characters switch between a letters set and a figures set. Each character is framed by a start bit and a stop bit so the receiver knows where it begins and ends. Baudot has no error detection or correction.

RTTY is sent with frequency shift keying. The two frequencies are called mark and space, names inherited from the old wired telegraph and teleprinter days. On ham HF RTTY they are usually 170 Hz apart.

concepts.title: PSK31 and Varicode
body: PSK31 is a narrow keyboard-to-keyboard mode running at 31.25 symbols per second. It sends characters in Varicode, a code in which characters have different lengths, much like Morse code. The most common characters, the lowercase letters such as e and t, get the shortest codes.

Uppercase letters are less common in normal text, so they get longer bit sequences. Typing in all capitals therefore slows PSK31 down. Capitals are not sent with more power; every bit goes out at the same level.
Plain (BPSK) PSK31 has no error correction, yet because it is so narrow it copies well with less power than RTTY needs for the same error rate.

concepts.title: Weak-signal modes: WSPR and FT8
body: Some digital modes are designed to be decoded when the signal is far below the noise you could hear. They trade speed for sensitivity: slow, narrow transmissions with strong error correction.

WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter, said like whisper) is a low-power beacon mode. Stations send short, very narrow transmissions with their call, grid square, and power, often at a watt or less. Receiving stations upload what they hear to the internet, giving a live map of where each band is open. It is a tool for assessing HF propagation, not for conversation.

FT8 sends brief structured exchanges in 15-second slots and can decode signals with a very low signal-to-noise ratio, around −20 dB. Its reports are signal-to-noise ratios in dB, measured as if in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth (roughly an SSB channel). So +3 means 3 dB above the noise in that bandwidth, not an S-meter reading. Other modes such as MSK144 (meteor scatter) and AMTOR are not built for this kind of deep weak-signal work.

concepts.title: Packets, headers, and ARQ
body: Packet modes split data into frames. Each frame has a header at the front with the routing and handling information: who it is from, who it is going to, and the path it should take. The data follows, then a checksum the receiver uses to spot errors.

ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) modes check each packet on arrival. If it arrived intact, the receiver sends an ACK (acknowledge). If it was damaged, the receiver sends a NAK (negative acknowledge), asking for that packet to be sent again.
Retries cannot go on forever. If conditions are so poor that too many attempts fail, the software gives up and the connection is dropped.

concepts.title: Forward error correction
body: Forward error correction (FEC) fixes errors without asking for a repeat. The sender transmits redundant information along with the data, extra bits calculated from the message. If some bits are damaged, the receiver uses the redundancy to work out what they must have been.
FEC works well on one-way or broadcast transmissions and in modes like FT8 and QPSK31. A single parity bit is not FEC: it can only tell you that a character has an error, not which bit to fix.

concepts.title: Mesh networks and digital voice
body: A ham mesh network (such as AREDN) links many microwave nodes, each one able to pass traffic for the others. The network finds routes on its own, so if one node fails, a packet can still reach its destination through an alternate node. Adding nodes adds paths; it does not make any individual signal stronger. Nodes that talk to each other directly over RF must share the same channel and bandwidth.

Digital voice modes turn speech into data before sending it. The three common systems on VHF and UHF are DMR, D-STAR, and System Fusion (Yaesu's C4FM). Don't confuse these with data modes: WSPR and FT8 are weak-signal modes, Winlink and PACTOR carry email and files, and EasyPAL sends pictures.

concepts.title: Reading a waterfall display
body: A waterfall display is how most digital-mode software shows the band. Frequency runs horizontally across the screen. Time runs vertically, with new lines appearing at one edge and older ones scrolling away like falling water. Signal strength is shown by intensity or color, so a stronger signal is a brighter streak.

A clean data or RTTY signal shows as a neat trace (or pair of traces for RTTY). Extra vertical lines on either side of it are unwanted products from overmodulation, usually too much audio drive into the transmitter. Turn the audio level down until they disappear.

G8A01.why: Direct FSK shifts the transmitter's own oscillator between two frequencies under control of the digital signal. That differs from audio FSK, which feeds tones into an SSB transmitter; sub-audible tones and CW key inputs have nothing to do with it.

G8A02.why: Changing the phase angle of a signal to carry information is phase modulation. Phase inversion is a flip of 180 degrees, not a name for a modulation process.

G8A03.why: Varying the instantaneous frequency of the wave to carry information is frequency modulation. Frequency conversion is tempting, but that is what a mixer does to move a signal to a new frequency.

G8A04.why: A reactance modulator on an RF amplifier stage shifts the phase of the signal passing through, so it produces phase modulation. The same circuit on the oscillator itself would produce true FM.

G8A05.why: Amplitude modulation varies the strength of the RF wave, so its instantaneous power rises and falls with the audio. There is no mode called power modulation, and FM and PM keep the amplitude constant.

G8A06.why: QPSK31 has all three traits. Both stations must use the same sideband because four-phase signals get mirrored between sidebands, it adds error-correcting code, and it runs at the same symbol rate and nearly the same bandwidth as BPSK31.

G8A07.why: Single sideband sends only one copy of the audio with no carrier, so it is the narrowest phone mode at about 3 kHz. Vestigial sideband keeps part of the second sideband, and FM and PM are several times wider.

G8A08.why: Overmodulation distorts the signal, and the distortion creates extra frequencies on both sides of it. The signal spreads out and becomes too wide, causing splatter on nearby frequencies.

G8A09.why: FT8 uses 8-tone frequency shift keying, with each symbol being one of eight closely spaced tones. It is not a sideband or spread spectrum mode.

G8A10.why: Flat-topping happens when too much drive or microphone gain pushes the peaks past what the amplifier can produce, so they are clipped flat. That is distortion, a sign that something is set wrong, not a sign that the ALC is working properly.

G8A11.why: The modulation envelope is the outline you get by connecting the peaks of the modulated RF waveform. It traces the shape of the audio riding on the carrier.

G8A12.why: QPSK uses four phase states, 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees, and each one stands for a pair of bits. The other choices are made-up descriptions that sound technical.

G8A13.why: A link budget starts with transmit power, adds the antenna gains, and subtracts all the losses to find what power actually reaches the receiver. Leaving out the transmit power, as in the sum of antenna gains minus losses, misses the starting point.

G8A14.why: Link margin is how far the received power is above the minimum signal level the receiver needs. Transmit power minus receiver sensitivity is tempting, but it ignores the antenna gains and path losses in between.

G8B01.why: The IF stays fixed, so the receiver tunes by changing the local oscillator. Each new LO setting converts a different incoming frequency to the IF. The beat frequency oscillator is used later, to demodulate CW and SSB.

G8B02.why: A signal on the opposite side of the local oscillator, twice the IF away from the desired signal, produces the same IF output. Interference from it is called image response.

G8B03.why: Mixing two RF signals to produce sum and difference frequencies is called heterodyning. It is the idea behind the superheterodyne receiver.

G8B04.why: A multiplier stage produces a harmonic of a lower-frequency signal, for example 12 times the oscillator frequency, to reach the VHF operating frequency. A mixer produces sums and differences rather than harmonics.

G8B05.why: Odd-order products such as 2F1 − F2 land just beside the original signals, often inside the same band. Even-order products fall far away, near double the frequencies or at the difference between them.

G8B06.why: By Carson's rule, add the deviation and the modulating frequency, then double the total for both sides of center. 8 kHz is the tempting wrong answer, because it forgets the doubling.

G8B07.why: The 12.21 MHz oscillator is multiplied 12 times to reach 146.52 MHz, and the deviation is multiplied along with it. So the oscillator only needs one-twelfth of the final 5 kHz deviation.

G8B08.why: Modes like FM, RTTY, and FT8 hold the transmitter at full output for the whole transmission. That high duty cycle can exceed an average power rating built with low-duty-cycle SSB voice in mind, so you may need to reduce power.

G8B09.why: A receiver bandwidth wider than the signal only lets in extra noise, and a narrower one cuts off part of the signal. Matching them gives the best signal-to-noise ratio. No FCC rule requires it.

G8B10.why: Sending symbols faster means the signal changes more quickly, and a faster-changing signal occupies more spectrum. So higher symbol rates require wider bandwidth.

G8B11.why: A mixer produces the sum and the difference of its LO and RF input frequencies. The receiver then selects one of them, usually the difference, as the IF.

G8B12.why: When signals mix in a non-linear circuit and produce unwanted spurious outputs, that is intermodulation. Heterodyning is the same kind of mixing done on purpose to get a wanted output.

G8B13.why: Add the multipliers to find each product's order. 2F1 − F2 is third order, which is odd. The other two products listed are both even order, so it is the only odd-order product.

G8C02.why: WSPR is a low-power beacon mode. Stations around the world report what they decode, which shows where HF bands are open. PSK31 and MFSK16 are conversational modes, not beacons.

G8C03.why: The header at the start of each packet frame holds the routing and handling information, such as the source, destination, and path. A preamble only helps the receiver synchronize before the frame arrives.

G8C04.why: Baudot code uses 5 bits per character, framed by start and stop bits. It has no parity or error correction; the 7-bit code with parity describes ASCII.

G8C05.why: A NAK (negative acknowledgment) tells the sender that the packet arrived damaged and must be sent again. A good packet gets an ACK instead.

G8C06.why: When conditions are so poor that too many retries fail, the ARQ system gives up and the connection is dropped. Nothing overflows or gets rerouted.

G8C07.why: FT8 is built to decode signals far below the noise, around −20 dB signal-to-noise ratio. MSK144 is a fast meteor-scatter mode, and AMTOR and MFSK32 need much stronger signals.

G8C08.why: Varicode gives the shortest codes to common lowercase letters, so uppercase letters take longer bit sequences and slow the transmission. Every bit is sent at the same power, and plain PSK31 needs less power than RTTY and has no error correction.

G8C09.why: A mesh network finds its own routes, so if one node fails, traffic can go around it through another node. Adding nodes adds paths but does not make signals stronger.

G8C10.why: FEC sends redundant information along with the data, which lets the receiver rebuild bits that were damaged without asking for a repeat. A single parity bit can only detect an error, not correct it.

G8C11.why: The two frequencies of an FSK signal are called mark and space, names that date back to the telegraph and teleprinter.

G8C12.why: PSK31 sends characters in Varicode, where common characters get short codes and rare ones get long codes. Viterbi is the name of a decoding method used with error-correcting codes, not a character code.

G8C13.why: Extra vertical lines beside a data or RTTY trace on a waterfall are spurious products from overmodulation, usually too much audio drive. Propagation effects would not show up as neat lines on each side.

G8C14.why: On a waterfall, frequency runs across the screen, time scrolls vertically, and signal strength shows as brightness or color.

G8C15.why: FT8 reports are signal-to-noise ratios in dB, measured as if in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth. A report of +3 means the signal is 3 dB above the noise in that bandwidth. It is not an S-meter reading.

G8C16.why: DMR, D-STAR, and System Fusion are the three common digital voice systems. The other groups are data modes: weak-signal modes, email and file systems, and picture modes.
